problem: Deep RL navigation agents were trained and evaluated in simplified environments such as mazes, DeepMind Lab and VizDoom, or were tested only on pixel-level variations. They overfit to their training scenes and fail on unseen environments with different layouts, objects and appearances. No environment was at once large-scale, realistic, fast and customizable enough to study semantic-level generalization.
motivation: A useful household navigation agent (e.g. 'go to the kitchen') must generalize to new houses. That requires robustness to low-level variation (color, texture) and to high-level variation (layout, furniture). The authors observe that generalization needs augmentation at several levels (pixel, task, scene), and that SUNCG's 45K fully labeled human-designed houses make all of these possible if they are turned into a fast interactive simulator.
key_idea: The paper builds House3D, a fast OpenGL simulator over 45,622 labeled SUNCG houses. It defines the RoomNav concept-driven navigation task and shows that gated-attention RL agents generalize to unseen houses only when pixel-level (domain randomization / segmentation masks), task-level (multi-target) and scene-level (many training houses) augmentations are combined.
insight:
Overfitting, not optimization, is the main obstacle. On the 20-house set with RGB input, gated-LSTM reaches higher training success but lower test success than concat-LSTM, because it latches onto spurious color cues. Ablations show that the three augmentation levels act on different causes of overfitting and add up:
- Domain randomization (180 recolored copies of the small set) gives test success similar to feeding semantic masks.
- Training on 15 auxiliary object targets mainly helps high-capacity gated models on RGB, and helps little with mask input.
- Scene diversity (200 houses) largely closes the train/test gap for every model.
- On the large set, recurrent LSTM policies beat reactive 5-frame CNNs, suggesting diverse scenes force the agent to learn exploration and memory rather than memorize actions.
- An auxiliary room-type prediction task did not help; the authors attribute this to the strong shortest-distance reward shaping.
method: House3D environment: an OpenGL renderer over the SUNCG houses providing RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, top-down occupancy maps, connectivity and shortest paths. It renders 120×90 frames at over 600 fps per renderer, up to 1800 fps per M40 GPU. Collision uses a robot radius; doors and arches are passable.

RoomNav task: 'go to X' for 5 room types over 270 manually selected houses (E_small 20 / E_large 200 / E_test 50, disjoint). Success requires being inside the target room and seeing a designated associated object (≥4% of pixels) for 2 consecutive steps, within 100 steps.
Reward shaping (training only): the difference in approximate shortest distance to the target room, plus −0.3 collision penalty, +10 success reward and −0.1 per step outside the target room.

Gated-attention fusion: the concept embedding (dim 25) is mapped by an MLP/linear layer to the image-feature dimension, and the CNN feature is multiplied by sigmoid(·) elementwise. Concatenation fusion (concat-*) serves as the comparison.

Gated-LSTM + A3C (discrete): a per-frame CNN (4 conv layers 64/64/128/128, k5 s2, BN, 256-d FC) feeds the gated fusion, which is concatenated with the target and passed to a 256-d LSTM. Policy and value MLPs read [h_t, o_t]. The action space has 12 discrete actions (8 moves at 2 scales/diagonals, 4 rotations). Training uses 120–200 processes and 10^5 updates.

Gated-CNN + DDPG (continuous): 5 stacked frames go through a CNN (512-d), gated fusion and an MLP with Gumbel-Softmax. The output is bounded continuous velocity (x±0.5·(m1−m2), y±0.5·(m3−m4), ρ±30·(r1−r2)). A shared actor-critic uses gated fusion of the feature with the action for Q (SVG(0)-like).

Multi-level augmentation:
- Pixel level: random object recoloring (domain randomization) or GT segmentation-mask input.
- Task level: 15 extra object concepts (sofa, toilet, bed, etc.) as auxiliary targets.
- Scene level: 200 training houses instead of 20.

setting.backbone: gated-LSTM (4-layer CNN + 256-d LSTM, trained from scratch with A3C); gated-CNN (4-layer CNN, trained from scratch with DDPG)
setting.training_data: Online RL in House3D on 20 (E_small) or 200 (E_large) SUNCG houses with shaped rewards. Variants add 180 domain-randomized recolored copies of E_small, or 15 auxiliary object-concept targets. DDPG runs 80,000 episodes; A3C runs 10^5 updates.
setting.observation: egocentric first-person 120×90 images: RGB, RGB+Depth, or semantic segmentation mask + Depth; target concept as one-hot
setting.action_space: 12 discrete actions (8 movements at two scales incl. diagonals, 4 rotations; |δx|,|δy|≤0.5, |δρ|≤30°) for A3C; continuous bounded velocity (4 movement + 2 rotation components) for DDPG; 100-step budget
setting.privileged: Mask+Depth variants (including the best 35.8% model) use ground-truth semantic segmentation masks from the simulator at test time. Shortest-distance reward shaping is used only during training.

numbers.extra: GT segmentation mask + depth input; trained on 200 houses (E_large); 50 held-out test houses, 2000 eval episodes, 100-step budget

numbers_note: Most results (training and test success on E_small and E_large for all input modalities, models, augmentations and auxiliary targets) are shown only as bar charts in Figs. 3–5, without printed values. The text gives a baseline of 25.7% ('10% better than the baseline method (25.7%)') but does not state its exact configuration; it is likely an RGB-input model, and it is not included above. Table 4 reports only average steps-to-success for successful episodes, e.g. gated-LSTM Mask+Depth test on E_large 34.3 steps. The benchmark is the paper's own RoomNav task on a custom 50-house test split; no SPL is reported.
results: The best agent, gated-LSTM with Mask+Depth trained on 200 houses, reaches 35.8% success on 50 unseen houses. This is about 10 points above the 25.7% baseline and over 8% better than RGB-input models and the same model trained on 20 houses. Gated-CNN (DDPG) reaches 29.7%. The augmentations are complementary: training on E_large consistently improves test success for every model and shrinks the train/test gap. Per-concept, dining and living rooms are easiest (~42–54%) and bathroom is hardest (17–21%).
limitations: SUNCG houses are synthetic CAD scenes, and the strongest agent relies on ground-truth segmentation masks at test time. There is no sim-to-real or real-robot validation.

Absolute success is low (35.8%). Training depends on strong privileged shortest-distance reward shaping, and results are mostly given as bar charts on a custom 270-house subset with no path-efficiency metric (SPL).
Interaction is limited to collision-free navigation (no manipulation), and only 5 room-type goals are evaluated.
